Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
658 AM EDT Mon Sep 21 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 253 AM EDT Monday...

No significant changes with this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 253 AM EDT Monday...

1. Tranquil weather conditions expected through mid week, with 
patchy frost possible tonight and Tuesday night. 

2. While high pressure and cool weather may continue into the 
weekend, a low pressure system will approach southern New England 
and potentially bring us periods of rain.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 253 AM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A cold front will continue to cross the region early 
this morning. In the meantime, patchy dense fog, drizzle, and dreary 
skies will linger through sunrise. Conditions will then slowly 
improve through the day as drier air flows in behind the frontal 
boundary. While not as chilly and damp as yesterday, north winds 
will be a touch brisk with highs only getting into the mid 50s to 
low 60s. 

The remainder of the first half of the week will feature fair 
weather as high pressure settles to our north, keeping developing 
low pressure and its associated precipitation shunted well to our 
south. The result will be partly to mostly sunny skies and 
seasonably cool temperatures each day. There will be a slight 
warming trend through Thursday, with highs mainly in the 60s. Lows 
will be in the upper 30s to low 40s each night, except in the 
sheltered valleys of the Adirondacks, Northeast Kingdom, and eastern 
VT, where temperatures will dip into the low to mid 30s. This will 
allow for patchy frost; subsequent shifts will need to monitor the 
potential for Frost Advisories. It should be noted that, as of 
today, these products will no longer be issued for the 
Adirondacks/Northeast Kingdom since today is the median date of the 
first autumn freeze. Thus, the growing season is considered ended in 
these areas.

KEY MESSAGE 2: No significant impacts are expected, but a beneficial 
rainfall is on the table for the upcoming weekend. The Friday 
through Sunday period remains highly uncertain for sensible weather. 
There is potential for dry weather to continue, but also a chance 
for widespread rain to occur, associated with an expected deep low 
pressure system that tracks northward over the western Atlantic 
Ocean. The 48 hour probability of precipitation from the blend of 
models suggests some rain is likely across south central Vermont and 
the Upper Valley, which has trended upward compared to 12 hours ago 
but similar to 24 hours ago. Otherwise, a coin flip chance across 
the rest of northern Vermont and northeastern New York as far north 
as near Plattsburgh continues, and a low (under 25%) chance of any 
rain is indicated to the northwest towards the International Border 
and St. Lawrence Valley. 

There have been many runs of deterministic guidance from both the 
GFS and ECMWF showing deformation bands of rain translating 
northward across much of Vermont, pinwheeling westward and then 
contracting back towards the south as surface low pressure stalls 
out/retrogrades and weakens in the Saturday-Saturday night 
timeframe. This idea is reflected in the six hour PoP trend, with 
most widespread low chances of rain centered in the Saturday morning 
period. Moderate rainfall amounts are possible given this type of 
system, especially in our southern and eastern areas. The 90th 
percentile (reasonable high end) shows near 1" totals possible in 
central Vermont increasing to near 2" in our far southern areas. 
Again, this type of rain would not pose any hazards but would 
obviously impact weekend outdoor activities. 

Additionally, the higher terrain, especially in the central/southern 
Greens, may see unseasonably strong winds with 40 to 45 MPH easterly 
winds at the 850 millibar level indicated by the mean of the 
ensemble guidance that shows the wetter/more northward low track 
amongst the possible scenarios. So potentially hazardous 
recreational conditions, when combined with rain and temperatures in 
the 40s, will be present this weekend. Otherwise, aside from cooler 
conditions associated with any rain, consistent temperatures near 
seasonable values should continue into the weekend.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Through 12Z Tuesday...A wide range in flight conditions
continues. IFR conditions at MPV/EFK/BTV/RUT are likely to 
improve within the 12Z to 15Z period. North winds will be
generally 5-9 knots, except around 10-12 knots at BTV and PBG, 
for much of the daytime period before becoming light. Limited
chances for recurrence of fog/stratus tonight with lower surface
moisture and continued drying northerly flow off the deck. 

Outlook...

Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Friday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&

.MARINE...
As of 253 AM EDT Monday...Near Lake Wind Advisory criteria will be in
place early this morning as cold air advection develops with a
cold frontal passage. North winds will generally remain 15 to 20
kt, but a few gusts to 25 kt are possible, especially across 
the central and southern portion of the broad lake and down 
towards Diamond Island. Wave heights in this region should reach
2-4 feet between 6 am and 10 am before subsiding this 
afternoon.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
